LEHRP · Water Pathway Audit · September 2026

The Purple-Pipe Loop

Ladera Ranch's drainage is captured at the Horno Basin and re-sprayed on the community through the purple-pipe recycled-water system. This report maps that loop from official sources and aerial imagery, then audits a community-raised theory: that pesticides, pharmaceuticals, and untested legacy arsenic could recirculate and compound in it.

Read this first. This is an independent research and data-organization project. It does not provide medical advice and does not establish that any party caused any illness. No contaminant is asserted to be present in any water or soil discussed here; the relevant streams have not been publicly tested for the constituents examined, which is itself a central finding. Every claim carries a statement class (verified fact, official statement, scientific finding, model estimate, inference, hypothesis, missing evidence). Geographic and temporal overlap does not establish exposure or causation.

1 · The loop is real — verified

The water district's own materials establish the geometry A2:

» The district "collects urban return (runoff) water from Oso Creek, Dove Creek, and Horno Creek to blend with the recycled water as an additional source for irrigation." (District recycled-water page.)

» The "Horno Basin... designed to capture, treat and deliver millions of gallons of runoff water for local irrigation use." (District newsletter, May 2012, archived with hash.)

The delivery network is the community's purple-pipe system — the lavender-colored piping that industry-wide marks recycled, non-potable water. It irrigates the slopes, parks, medians, and common-area turf of Ladera Ranch. So water that drains off the community's landscapes is captured at the bottom of the watershed and a portion of it is sprayed back onto those same landscapes. That is not a theory; it is the design intent, stated by its operator.

2 · The audit — what fails, what survives

The theory as raised: constituents "build up" because the basin "does not treat for those chemicals," making "one big ongoing toxic loop that compounds." We stress-tested each clause.

FAILS AUDIT — "compounds" in the water. The loop is partial, not closed. Storm flows bypass the capture (dry-weather diversions take low flows only); evapotranspiration removes water; irrigation blends captured runoff into a much larger recycled+imported supply; some water infiltrates. A steady-state recirculation model Model estimate caps water-phase enrichment even under generous assumptions:

ScenarioRunoff fraction fCapture cPass-through rWater multiplier
Conservative0.080.400.50×1.02
Moderate0.150.600.70×1.07
Aggressive upper bound0.300.800.90×1.28
Fully closed loop (impossible)0.501.001.00×2.00

Runaway concentration in the water supply is not physically supported. Reporting otherwise would be sensationalism, and it would be wrong.

SURVIVES AUDIT — redistribution. The loop's real significance is geographic: whatever the drainage carries — dissolved or fine-particulate — gets pumped back uphill and sprayed across every purple-pipe-irrigated surface in the community. A constituent that started in one place ends up everywhere the sprinklers reach. Inference from verified geometry

SURVIVES AUDIT — accumulation in soil. Irrigation water evaporates; persistent constituents do not. Metals (arsenic among them) and persistent pesticide residues left behind by each cycle accumulate in landscape soils roughly linearly with years of application — independent of the loop's water-phase gain. Two-plus decades of purple-pipe irrigation is two-plus decades of deposition. Magnitude: unmeasured. Scientific principle + missing evidence

SURVIVES AUDIT — the treatment gap, as an open question. Basin-level urban-runoff facilities of this type are engineered for trash, sediment, and gross solids; dissolved metals and dissolved organics largely pass filtration B1 — general engineering literature. Tertiary treatment at the Chiquita plant (Title 22) removes pathogens and solids and only partially removes pharmaceuticals and other trace organics B1. Whether THIS basin's works remove any dissolved constituent is documented in the engineer-of-record drawings and the district's permit file — both obtainable by public-records request, neither yet in hand. Missing evidence

3 · The chemicals, taken one at a time

ConstituentEnters the loop howEvidence status
Landscape pesticides (fipronil, pyrethroids)Applied on HOA/residential landscaping; wash off in irrigation runoff — the classic Southern California urban-runoff signalPresence in regional urban runoff: B1. Levels in THIS loop: untested
Pharmaceuticals / trace organicsSurvive tertiary treatment in part; enter via the recycled-water blendPhenomenon: B1. Levels in this blend: not publicly reported
Arsenic (legacy, 1907–1912 era)IF present in drainage soils (unmeasured), mobilizes in runoff as dissolved and fine-particulate phases; filtration does not remove the dissolved phaseHypothesis — no soil or runoff arsenic data exists for this watershed; the historical program on this land is documented A1

On "never tested": the district's drinking water is tested and reports arsenic at non-detect to trace levels — that system is separate and not at issue here. What has no public testing record is the captured-runoff stream, the basin sediment, and the irrigated landscape soils — the loop itself. That gap is the finding.

4 · The endpoints, from the air

VERDICT ON THE THEORY

Not supported as stated: "one big ongoing toxic loop that compounds" — the water-phase compounding fails a straightforward mass-balance audit, and honesty about that is what keeps the rest credible.

Supported, restated defensibly: Ladera Ranch operates a documented capture-and-respray loop through its purple-pipe system. That loop redistributes whatever the community's drainage carries onto its landscapes, deposits persistent constituents into landscape soils year after year, and does so with no public monitoring of the captured-runoff stream for pesticides, pharmaceuticals, or legacy arsenic — on land where a federal arsenical dipping program operated a century ago and where soil has never been tested for it. The reported pattern warrants investigation; the current data are insufficient to determine whether any constituent is present at levels of concern.

5 · What would settle it — four inexpensive samples

#SampleWhat it answers
1Irrigation water at a purple-pipe sprinkler head (arsenic + speciation, pesticide panel, CEC screen)What the loop is actually delivering today — the single cheapest, highest-value test
2Horno Basin sediment coreWhat the watershed has been shedding, time-resolved
3Long-irrigated turf/slope soil vs. never-irrigated controlWhether two decades of spray built a measurable soil deposit
4Blend-point water at the tank/plant (pending as-builts)Which route the water takes and what treatment it actually receives

Item 4's prerequisite — the engineer-of-record as-built drawings — is one public-records request to the water district. Draft prepared.
